transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Kira Patel (Redwood Infra), Priya Kumar (CTO - Hypersight), Jon Lee (ML Eng - Hypersight), Marcus Reed (Security Lead - Hypersight), Elena Park (Product PM - Hypersight)

[00:00] Alice Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? We'll focus today on prefix, uh, pre-fix caching strategy and safety model, and how that fits into VPC/private setups. Marco and Kira from our infra team will handle the deep bits.
[00:18] Priya Kumar: Thanks Alice. We're most interested in reducing token cost and improving p95 latency for our product search flows. We have a lot of identical system prompts and user prefixes across queries.
[00:30] Marco Diaz: Great, so typical scenario: if you have a stable system prompt + initial context that repeats, prefix caching can get a large headstart - we cache the KV cache for that prefix and resume generation. In our experience hit rates vary wildly based on reuse; for high-reuse templates we see 40-70% logical hit rates, for more dynamic prompts it can drop under 20%.
[00:55] Jon Lee: When you say hit-rate, is that for exact-match keys? We have small personalization tokens appended, so we need per-user parts not to poison the cache.
[01:10] Marco Diaz: Yes mostly exact-match keys; cache keys are critical. We usually recommend composing the key from a stable fingerprint: model name + model version + normalized system prompt + conversation prefix up to N tokens + temperature/decoding params + tenant id namespace. Personalization fields should be excluded or hashed out into a separate dynamic layer.
[01:34] Marcus Reed: How do you prevent cross-tenant leakage on the hosted side? Our security team won't accept any chance of leaked KV shards.
[01:44] Kira Patel: We scope caches by tenant namespace - at the Redis or in-memory layer we prefix keys with tenant IDs and optional instance IDs. For multi-tenant hosted, we also support per-tenant encryption keys (KMS) for at-rest cache entries and strict RBAC on the cache control plane. For private/VPC customers, cache can run inside the same VPC and be customer-managed.
[02:06] Priya Kumar: What's the tradeoff on storage vs hit-rate? If we keep large prefixes we get better hits but more memory.
[02:16] Marco Diaz: Exactly. Eviction policies and TTL tuning is essential. We typically keep a rolling LRU with tiered TTLs: short TTLs for very high churn prefixes, longer for stable templates. Also consider prefix bucketing: only cache prefixes up to, say, 256 tokens or compress the fingerprints. In practice at scale we target a 1-2% of total model state memory per active customer for prefix cache - but it's workload-dependent.
[02:50] Jon Lee: On the infra side, is the KV cache colocated on the same GPU host or is it an external service? Latency matters for p95.
[03:00] Kira Patel: Two options. 1) Local in-process/in-host KV cache: extremely low latency (single-digit ms), best for Dedicated or Private where you can guarantee isolation. 2) External cache (Redis/managed): easier horizontal scaling, faster to share across replicas, but adds network hop; p95 impact depends on network and region - typically adds 5-15ms. For hosted we sometimes use a hybrid: local ephemeral cache for hot prefixes plus Redis as a cold store.
[03:30] Elena Park: If we run in our VPC, we can host Redis ourselves. Any special config?
[03:37] Kira Patel: Standard: ensure Redis AUTH, TLS in transit, VPC endpoints, and network policies to restrict access. For hypersight private install we can optionally mount the cache inside the inference container or use a co-located statefulset. Also note persistence: caches are usually ephemeral but you can snapshot if you want fast warm restarts.
[03:59] Marcus Reed: What about the risk of poisoning or serving wrong content because of stale cached KV?
[04:07] Marco Diaz: That's on the design of cache key and TTL. If two prefixes only differ in a small personalization token and you accidentally canonicalize them the wrong way you can return incorrect output. So we recommend strict canonicalization rules and conservative TTLs when personalization fields are involved. Also we provide an invalidation API so customers can invalidate keys on user update events.
[04:33] Priya Kumar: How does prefix caching interact with batching? Our traffic bursts, and batching is key for throughput.
[04:42] Marco Diaz: Good question. Batching combines multiple requests into a single forward pass; cache hits shorten the prefix that needs to be processed, which can actually improve batching efficiency because shorter prefix processing reduces token work before requests join the dynamic batch for generation. However, cache-hit variability can increase tail latency if some requests need a long prefix recompute. Our runtime uses workload-aware batching heuristics: we separate warm (cache-hit) and cold (miss) requests into different pipelines when possible to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[05:12] Jon Lee: Any numbers you can share for hit vs latency?
[05:16] Marco Diaz: Example from a retailer workload: baseline generation p95 420ms without caching; with prefix caching + good hit rate (~55%) we saw p95 drop to ~210ms and throughput up by ~1.6x. For smaller models or shorter sequences gains are less dramatic but still meaningful. Quantization can also change per-token times - int8 kernels reduce per-token latency by ~20-35% depending on hardware.
[05:46] Priya Kumar: We use some quantized models internally. Any compatibility issues between quantized kernels and KV cache?
[05:54] Kira Patel: KV cache is model-architecture agnostic but the binary layout of the KV tensors must match the runtime. If you swap to a different quantized backend or model variant, you must invalidate or namespace the cache by model+quantization profile. We include the quantization schema in the cache key to avoid mismatches.
[06:14] Elena Park: Are you storing raw token embeddings in the cache or a serialized format?
[06:19] Marco Diaz: Serialized tensors with a compact binary representation - in some deployments we also store compressed float16 or quantized versions to save memory. For multi-tenant hosted services we never store plaintext PII in cache; we either strip or hash sensitive fields before caching.
[06:36] Marcus Reed: On compliance: do you provide audit logs for cache access and invalidations?
[06:42] Kira Patel: Yes, we can emit audit logs for cache operations (hits/misses/invalidate) to your logging endpoint or our console; retention is configurable. For Private installs we can integrate with customer SIEM.
[06:55] Priya Kumar: For our product, most of the heavy reuse is at the system-prompt + template level; per-user personalization is small. Could we do a two-tier approach?
[07:04] Marco Diaz: That's exactly what we recommend: tier 1 is global template prefix cache (shared across tenants if allowed, otherwise per-tenant), tier 2 is per-user delta layer applied after retrieval. So you fetch the shared prefix KV then apply user-specific tokens. This keeps memory efficient and safe.
[07:25] Jon Lee: Any concerns around deterministic outputs when using cached KV?
[07:30] Marco Diaz: Cache should be deterministic as long as model, decoding params, and prefix are identical. Non-determinism from sampling params (temperature, top-k) is why we include those in the key. For safety you can set deterministic decoding for cached prefixes if you need reproducibility.
[07:48] Priya Kumar: What about cache warm-up? If we deploy a new model or version, how do we prime the cache?
[07:55] Kira Patel: Several strategies: 1) offline warm-up by replaying top N historical prefixes; 2) on-demand warm-up where first requests are handled with a warm-up pool; 3) seed the cache with synthetic canonical prefixes from your templates. We'll help coordinate replay pipelines.
[08:15] Elena Park: In terms of cost, what's the ballpark for adding prefix cache? Memory and infra costs?
[08:21] Marco Diaz: Memory cost is proportional to cache size - e.g., for a small team you might add a few GBs of managed cache; bigger enterprise may use tens of GB. Cost varies with whether it's in-host memory (higher host sizing) vs shared Redis. But most customers see net cost reduction because token savings outweigh cache infra costs.
[08:41] Marcus Reed: Do you have mitigations for cache poisoning or DOS on the cache store?
[08:47] Kira Patel: Rate-limit writes, authenticate and authorize clients, monitor abnormal key churn, and support per-tenant quotas. For hosted we run anomaly detectors and can throttle noisy tenants. Also provide signed cache keys to avoid arbitrary writes if you expose invalidate endpoints.
[09:05] Jon Lee: For private installs, is there a recommended config for eviction policy?
[09:10] Marco Diaz: We typically use LRU with weighted sizes based on prefix token length. TTLs vary; set longer TTLs for templates and short for interactive sessions. Also consider cold-store tiering: move older entries to a cheaper Redis cluster if you want to keep a large historical cold cache.
[09:28] Priya Kumar: Can you show us a proposed cache-key composition?
[09:31] Marco Diaz: Sure, high-level: SHA256(tenant_id || model_name || model_version || quant_profile || normalized_system_prompt || prefix_hash || decode_params) with optional namespace and timestamp segment for TTL buckets. Avoid including user-identifiers in the global key; instead include a per-user delta key if needed.
[09:58] Elena Park: How do you normalize system prompt? We have templates with whitespace and small variable markers.
[10:04] Marco Diaz: Normalize by canonicalizing whitespace, removing ephemeral tokens, replacing variable placeholders with stable markers, and optionally applying a regex to strip timestamps. We keep a documented normalization pipeline that you can customize.
[10:18] Alice Chen: Quick note: we'll include the normalization rules in the design doc.
[10:22] Priya Kumar: Any pitfalls we should watch for?
[10:25] Kira Patel: Common pitfalls: over-canonicalizing and accidentally merging distinct prompts; not namespacing cache keys by model/quant; ignoring TTL tuning; and failing to monitor hit/miss patterns which can lead to cache bloat.
[10:41] Jon Lee: For our bench, what metrics should we capture?
[10:45] Marco Diaz: Capture hit-rate (global and per-template), average and p95 latency for both hits and misses, token-savings (tokens avoided * token_cost), cache evictions/sec, and memory footprint. Also trace cold-start recompute times.
[11:00] Priya Kumar: OK that sounds good. On the privacy front, we can't allow any user-uploaded PII to be cached in plaintext.
[11:07] Kira Patel: We'll provide an option to scrub or hash PII fields before caching. For enterprises we recommend customer-managed KMS so stored caches are encrypted with customer keys.
[11:19] Alice Chen: Let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[11:23] Alice Chen: Action items: Alice will share design doc + pricing; Marco will run bench and share results; Kira will prepare security/on-prem notes; Jon will share sample prompts. We'll meet again on 2026-04-28 to review.
[11:37] Priya Kumar: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[11:40] Marco Diaz: Thanks all, we'll get the doc over.
[11:43] (call ends)
